blocks.content: Misreading a simple 'NOT' or 'INCORRECT' in a question stem is the single most common cause of negative marking in competitive examinations.

rows: Search for a single exception; extreme statements are usually false
Rephrase the question into a positive statement before answering
First half of option is correct, second half is wrong
Read every option completely from start to finish
Includes partial calculation results as choice options
Double-check that the final step of the formula was executed

items: Always circle or underline words like 'NOT', 'INCORRECT', and 'EXCEPT' immediately upon reading the question stem.
Verify the exact unit requested in quantitative questions before selecting your answer, as unconverted units are standard distractor choices.
Do not mark Option A immediately upon finding it plausible; always read options B, C, and D to prevent falling for half-truth traps.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Examiners frequently use extreme qualifiers like 'always', 'never', and 'exclusively' to craft false options.
Negation phrases in question stems (e.g., 'Which of the following is NOT correct?') trigger the majority of avoidable negative marks.
Partial correctness traps present options that are accurate in their first half but contain a subtle error at the end.
Distractor options often feature intermediate calculation values to catch candidates who stop solving early.
